opus-5.5.text:
I think the most rewarding part is that it closes a loop that used to feel very open. When I started working on Taichi, it was really out of my own frustration. I was doing research in physical simulation, things like the material point method, and I kept writing the same kind of high-performance code over and over. Sparse data structures, GPU kernels, all this low-level engineering that had very little to do with the actual physics I cared about. So I thought: why not build a language that lets me express what I really want and let the compiler handle the painful parts?

So when I use Taichi now and write something in maybe a hundred lines that would have taken me thousands of lines of CUDA before, and it just runs fast, there's a very personal satisfaction in that. It's like building a tool for your past self.

But honestly, what's even more rewarding is seeing *other* people use it. Researchers, students, artists, people I've never met, building simulations, visual effects, little games, things I never imagined. Sometimes someone shows me a demo and I think, wow, I didn't know Taichi could do that. That feeling, that the tool has grown beyond what I designed it for, is really special.

And there's also a kind of humility that comes with it. When you use your own language every day, you feel all its rough edges very directly. You can't blame anyone else. So it constantly pushes me to make it better, and I think that tight feedback loop between being a user and being the designer is something I really cherish.

r001.rationale: Hu describes writing in Taichi what would have taken thousands of lines of CUDA in about a hundred, with the compiler handling the painful low-level work, conveying that Taichi is easier to use.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the most rewarding part is watching other people do things with it that I never imagined. When I started Taichi, the motivation was very personal. I was doing physics simulation research, and I was tired of writing hundreds of lines of CUDA just to test one idea. I wanted something where I could express the math in a few lines of Python and still have it run fast on a GPU. So in the beginning, the reward was simple: my own research went faster.

But then the community started picking it up, and the use cases exploded. People were using it for fluid simulation, sure, but also for computer vision, robotics, rendering, even generative art. I remember seeing someone build a real-time ray tracer in a weekend, and another person simulating snow for a film project. I had no idea what they were working on, and yet the language was helping them. That's a very different feeling from publishing a paper. A paper gets cited. A tool gets used, every day, by people who have their own problems to solve.

There's also a more technical kind of satisfaction. When you design a language, you're constantly making trade-offs between expressiveness and performance, between simplicity and control. Every time I write Taichi code myself and the abstraction holds up, where I write what I mean and the compiler does the hard work, that's a small confirmation that the design decisions were right. And when it doesn't hold up, that's useful too. I feel the pain directly, as a user, and that pushes me to fix it.

And finally, I think it changed how I view my role. In graduate school, I measured myself by how much I personally could compute or simulate. Now I think more about leverage. If I can lower the barrier so that a student without a systems background can run a sparse simulation on a GPU in an afternoon, then I've multiplied what the whole field can do. That's what keeps me going.

r001.rationale: The response says Taichi let Hu express ideas in a few lines of Python instead of writing hundreds of lines of CUDA, and that this sped up his research. It does not clearly state that discovering Taichi was easier to use than CUDA was itself rewarding.

astra-6.text: There’s something very satisfying about using a tool you built to solve a problem you care about. You have an idea, express it in the language, and see it work—that makes all the effort behind the language feel worthwhile. And using it yourself gives you very direct feedback. You notice where things feel natural and where you’re still fighting the design. That becomes motivation to make it better.

r001.rationale: The response says using a language he built is satisfying and gives useful design feedback, but it does not state that Yuanming Hu finds it easier to use than CUDA.
